messages.author: 51b9e9969e604449
messages.subject: Fitting a model with 0 iterations
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm currently in the process of implementing Satorra and Bentler (2010)'s revised scaled chi-square difference test (cited at the end of this post) in R using lavaan, however I've run into a bit of a snag. Calculation of the statistic involves fitting the less restricted model to the data using the parameter estimates for the more restricted model as starting values, with 0 iterations. However, this run never converges, and thus, the chi-square value is not obtainable. I've been trying to find a work-around using the control= parameter, but have not had much luck. I do not have a strong understanding of what is actually going on under the hood of the control= parameter, and have mostly just been adjusting values haphazardly, hoping for a useful outcome.

Curiously, setting the abs.tol parameter to an arbitrarily large number forces the run to successfully converge after one iteration, and the value of the objective function is sometimes what I want it to be, but sometimes it is not.

Verbose=T printout for sample data set A:
Quasi-Newton steps using NLMINB:
Objective function  = 0.0105796021406972
Objective function  = 0.0110700819706291
Objective function  = 0.0105796021406972
convergence status (0=ok):  0 

Verbose=T printout for sample data set B:
Quasi-Newton steps using NLMINB:
Objective function  = 0.0124020538275791
Objective function  = 0.0122766670941705
Objective function  = 0.0122766670941705
convergence status (0=ok):  0

Fitting to data set A returns the starting values as parameter estimates, and returns the same chi-square and robust chi-square that EQS does (when mimic="EQS"), which is what I would like to see happen every time. Does anybody have any advice as to how I might go about guaranteeing the first outcome for all data sets? Possibly by either forcing lavaan to converge after 0 iterations, or by forcing the difference between objective function estimates to be arbitrarily small, such that 1 iteration is indistinguishable from 0?

I'm not sure how helpful it will be, but here is the syntax and data used:
http://pastebin.com/31Rrtwqb
https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/11692532/SB2M10runs.R
https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/11692532/sampledata.csv
https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/11692532/sampledata2.csv

Thanks in advance to anyone who is able to lend a hand.

Cheers,

Jordan

-----------------------------
Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. (2010). Ensuring Positiveness of The Scaled Difference Chi-Square Test Statistic. Psychometrika, 75(2), 243-248.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Fitting a model with 0 iterations
parts:
On 02/18/2014 07:34 AM, Jordan Brace wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
> I'm currently in the process of implementing Satorra and Bentler
> (2010)'s revised scaled chi-square difference test (cited at the end of
> this post) in R using lavaan

Perhaps I should point out that the anova() function (and in 0.5-16, the
lavTestLRT() function) has implemented the original formulas of Satorra
(2000), when the test statistics are scaled. It would seem that lavaan
is the only program doing this.

The Satorra & Bentler (2010) paper is just showing how to do this
(approximately) if you need use software without these capabilities...

And to use that other approximation (of Satorra & Bentler, 2001), you
need to use the (hidden in 0.5-15) SB.classic=TRUE flag.

In dev 0.5-16, the help page of lavTestLRT() contains the proper references.

> Calculation of the statistic involves fitting the less restricted model
> to the data using the parameter estimates for the more restricted model
> as starting values, with 0 iterations.

I see the problem. It has come up before (in the semTools package). I
can not think of a robust solution. Using the abs.tol parameter to
'force' convergence will not work in a reliable way.

If you still want to pursue this, let me know, and I will think about a
more general approach.

Yves.

Thank you so much for getting back to me. I am still hoping to pursue implementing the 2010 methodology, as I am involved in a project that is specifically examining the performance of the Satorra-Bentler 2001 and 2010 statistics (most of which has involved interfacing R with EQS, but I'm hoping to use R alone for the remainder if possible). I will, however, bring up the possibility of considering the Satorra 2000 statistic as well with my advisor, as I was not previously aware that it had been implemented in R. Thank you for bringing that to my attention. But yes, If you can think of a way to help us get the 0 iteration run for the 2010 test consistently, it would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,

Jordan
